transcript:
[00:00] Evan Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for making time; Evan from Redwood. we'll do quick intros and then dig into latency and throughput.
[00:12] Sofia Kim: Hi all, Sofia here, head of ML at Mariner. We're evaluating options for inference - hosted vs dedicated vs private - mostly for our new conversational payments assistant. latency is huge for our UX.
[00:25] Aaron Patel: Aaron, infra. I just wanna understand network needs and whether we need VPC or can use the hosted endpoint.
[00:34] Priya Nair: Priya, I'm the SE; I'll run through the performance questions and what we need to benchmark. quick question up front — do you have defined p95 targets?
[00:44] Rhiannon Moss: Rhiannon, PM. Our internal target: p95 under 200ms for short completion (<=64 tokens), and p95 under 1.2s for streamed responses up to ~512 tokens. those are aspirational.
[00:58] Tom Wei: Tom, SRE. Also curious about concurrency — we can get spikes when marketing sends emails. baseline is ~400 concurrent inference sessions, but peak could reach 1500.
[01:15] Evan Carter: great, that's super helpful. On Redwood side we typically map those requirements to two things: model choice/config (quantization, batching) and deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private). hosted can get you fast time-to-value but Dedicated gives you predictable tail latency under high concurrency.
[01:35] Priya Nair: Right, and we also look at prefix/KV cache and streaming token throughput. a lot depends on whether you need streaming token/sec for long responses. you mentioned 512 tokens — do most of your calls stream or are they single-shot completions?
[01:50] Sofia Kim: mix of both, ~60% short single-shot, 40% streaming long tails for receipts and explanations. we care a lot about p95 and jitter.
[02:02] Aaron Patel: let me add infra constraints: we prefer traffic to stay in our VPC, we have strict egress rules, and our security team prefers KMS integration for key management. can Redwood support that on Dedicated or Private?
[02:15] Evan Carter: yes — Dedicated supports customer VPC peering and KMS integrations. Private gives you customer-managed control plane and on-prem if needed. Hosted supports encryption at rest and in transit but not customer-managed KMS by default, though we have options for enterprise.
[02:30] Priya Nair: For latency numbers: for a 64-token completion on an A100-class or H100-class GPU in Dedicated, with small batch sizes and warmed KV cache, p95s under 120-180ms are common for many open models. hosted may be similar on average but can have higher tail when noisy neighbors spike.
[02:52] Rhiannon Moss: ok that ballpark helps. what's the tokens/sec for streaming? we need to ensure the assistant streams smoothly for longer answers.
[03:02] Priya Nair: Streaming throughput varies by model and quantization. on a single H100 with optimized kernels you might see 600-1400 tokens/sec for autoregressive decode for smaller models; larger models or higher precision drop token/sec. with batching and pipelining we can push effective throughput higher but latency tradeoffs exist.
[03:22] Tom Wei: that 600-1400 tokens/sec — is that per GPU or per instance? and how does concurrency map?
[03:30] Luis Gonzalez: Luis here. that's roughly tokens/sec per GPU inference instance. concurrency depends on how you shard requests across GPUs, connection multiplexing, and batching windows. in Dedicated we can provision enough GPUs to keep per-request latency at your p95 target even under 1500 concurrent sessions.
[03:50] Aaron Patel: can you share a simple formula to estimate required GPUs from concurrency, tokens/sec, and p95?
[03:58] Priya Nair: quick heuristic: required_token_capacity = average_tokens_per_second * concurrent_requests. then divide by tokens/sec per GPU for your model and quant profile. leave headroom for spikes — we recommend 1.3-1.5x. so if you have 400 concurrent and average streaming rate 20 tokens/sec = 8k tokens/sec needed; if GPU does 800 tokens/sec then you'd need ~10 GPUs, add headroom => 13-15 GPUs.
[04:30] Sofia Kim: got it. our average streaming rate is more like 10-30 tokens/sec depending on the card and prompt. our big ask is to see p95 and token/sec numbers running our prompt set.
[04:42] Evan Carter: absolutely. we'll build a benchmark harness — Priya will propose test cases. the benchmark will measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, concurrency saturation, and memory/kv cache hit rates.
[04:54] Rhiannon Moss: how long does a Dedicated pilot typically take? we want to evaluate cost, tail latency and ops burden.
[05:02] Evan Carter: we can spin a short Dedicated pilot in 2-4 weeks depending on procurement. Hosted pilot could be immediate. Private takes longer because of network and security approvals.
[05:15] Aaron Patel: in terms of security docs — we need SOC2 and network diagrams. also can you provide audit logs granularity?
[05:24] Evan Carter: yes, we'll send SOC2 report, our audit log retention options, and sample network diagrams. Dedicated and Private give more control over audit logs and retention policies.
[05:36] Priya Nair: one thing to watch: for short completion p95 you want to minimize batching windows (use small batch sizes or adaptive batching) and enable prefix cache for repeated prompts. that reduces tail significantly.
[05:50] Tom Wei: do you have examples of batch settings we should start with? we usually avoid batching to keep latency low but we understand cost wins.
[05:59] Luis Gonzalez: start with max_batch_size 8-16 and latency-bound window 10-20ms for short completions; for streaming longer responses use lower batch size but bigger queuing if cost is important. we'll try to tune in the pilot.
[06:16] Sofia Kim: what's the difference in SLOs between Hosted and Dedicated? like p95 is different?
[06:23] Evan Carter: Hosted has best-effort p95 SLAs publicly but enterprise Hosted customers can get improved commitments. Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets based on reserved capacity. we can include fallback model routing to keep tail down.
[06:38] Rhiannon Moss: fallback model routing? explain that a bit.
[06:42] Priya Nair: if your primary model is a large one that's slower in some cases, Redwood can automatically route to a compatible smaller model variant when latency or capacity is constrained. that keeps the application responsive; quality can be tuned via policies.
[06:58] Aaron Patel: that seems useful. any customer examples?
[07:01] Evan Carter: we've used that with fintech customers during big spikes — switch to a quantized variant or smaller model to preserve p95 under load.
[07:10] Tom Wei: how do you measure KV cache hit rates? we have a lot of repeated prefixes.
[07:15] Priya Nair: we instrument prefix/KV cache hits per route and provide dashboards — cache hit percentage, bytes saved, effective token reduction. for repeated user prompts we often see 30-60% effective token reduction depending on similarity.
[07:30] Sofia Kim: nice. for our prompts we expect high reuse. that will change the GPU sizing.
[07:36] Rhiannon Moss: what about quantization — do you recommend int8 or int4 for our use? we need to balance cost and low-latency quality.
[07:45] Priya Nair: int8 is a good baseline; int4 gives more cost upside but may regress on some instruction-following quality tests. Redwood Optimize provides model/quant recommendations by workload and we can run evals on your prompt set as part of the pilot.
[08:00] Aaron Patel: network latency from our VPC to Redwood endpoints — how much does that add?
[08:06] Luis Gonzalez: depends on region and peering. typical intra-region VPC peering adds 5-20ms. we can measure RTT during the pilot; Private/on-prem eliminates WAN RTT but has ops overhead.
[08:18] Sofia Kim: ok so for our 200ms p95 target for 64 tokens that likely requires Dedicated with peered VPC and tuned batching/kv cache?
[08:27] Evan Carter: That's a reasonable conclusion — Hosted might hit it in light load but Dedicated gives predictable tails at scale. we'll verify with benchmarks.
[08:36] Rhiannon Moss: let's talk about cost — any rough numbers? we want Hosted per-token vs Dedicated fixed monthly with GPU costs.
[08:44] Evan Carter: we'll send a pricing sheet. rough high level: Hosted per-token includes infra and ops; Dedicated is committed monthly for reserved GPUs and lower unit cost but requires commit. We'll include example scenarios based on the benchmark.
[08:57] Tom Wei: can you support canary rollouts and automatic fallback in Dedicated? we want safe deploys.
[09:03] Priya Nair: yes, Redwood Console supports canary/A-B rollouts, tracers and error analysis per-route. automatic fallback policies can route around overloaded variants.
[09:14] Sofia Kim: timeline wise, if we get the benchmark plan by Monday we can run internal approvals and hit a pilot start mid-April?
[09:22] Evan Carter: sounds good. we'll target to deliver benchmark plan and security docs by 2027-04-12.
[09:28] Aaron Patel: one last technical question — do you support pinned model versions and KV cache invalidation control? we need reproducibility for logging.
[09:37] Luis Gonzalez: yes, you can pin model version and control cache TTL/invalidations. all requests include trace IDs for auditability.
[09:46] Rhiannon Moss: ok great. any risks or gotchas we should call out?
[09:50] Priya Nair: main things: network egress and peering setup time, warm-up for KV cache, and tuning batching vs latency. also quantization quality tradeoffs.
[09:59] Sofia Kim: perfect. can you include recommended benchmark metrics in the plan? p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, jitter, CPU/GPU util, cache hit %, cost per 1M tokens.
[10:10] Evan Carter: yes, we'll include those.
[10:14] -- timestamp jumps here to cover the Q&A and deeper technical details --
[20:45] Priya Nair: (demo note) the harness will run three scenarios: short single-shot (<=64 tokens), medium stream (128-256 tokens), long stream (512 tokens) with concurrency steps at 50/200/400/800/1500. each step collects latencies, throughput, and model quality checks.
[21:05] Aaron Patel: we'll also provide a sample traffic histogram showing 70% under 64 tokens, 20% 128-256, 10% >256.
[21:17] Evan Carter: perfect — that will let us size for your real distribution and estimate cost.
[21:23] Rhiannon Moss: for the quality checks are you doing automated evals against our ground truth?
[21:28] Priya Nair: yes we'll run rouge/bertscore style checks and some human evals for a subset. we can also do regression alerts tied to your prompt set.
[21:39] Tom Wei: what's needed from our side to run an initial Dedicated pilot?
[21:44] Evan Carter: signed pilot contract, network peering info, sample prompts, and a contact for infra to open peering/whitelist.
[21:52] Sofia Kim: onboarding support during pilot?
[21:55] Evan Carter: dedicated SE support included for the pilot; post-plan we'll assign a solutions engineer for tuning.
[22:02] -- later in the call troubleshooting notes and some crosstalk --
[32:10] Priya Nair: small note on measurement noise: please run repeated runs and we'll average p95 across runs and report variance. some of our internal numbers can vary with model warmness.
[32:22] Aaron Patel: makes sense. also for cost modeling can you give worst-case with 1.5x headroom?
[32:28] Evan Carter: yes we'll provide both baseline and 1.3-1.5x headroom estimates.
[32:35] Rhiannon Moss: ok, recap?
[32:38] Evan Carter: Recap: Redwood to share benchmark plan + test harness (Priya), SOC2/security pack and network diagram (Evan), pricing for Hosted vs Dedicated pilot (Evan), schedule SE deep-dive week of 4/19 (Evan to propose times). Mariner to share prompts, traffic histogram, and peering constraints (Sofia/Aaron).
[32:59] Sofia Kim: that sounds right. thanks everyone.
[33:02] Tom Wei: thanks.
[33:04] Evan Carter: great — we'll follow up via email with the artifacts and invite for the deep-dive.
[33:10] Rhiannon Moss: good call.
[33:12] -- end call --
